doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Eddie Vinson, Cootie Williams band, Hodges and Benny Carter
summary: He explains Vinson as a blues player and songwriter, and recalls bands coming through Greensboro and playing Hodges solos.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: We were just discussing alto saxophonists. You mentioned Earl Bostic. But could you talk a bit about each of the people I mentioned, and how they affected you? Let’s say, Eddie “Cleanhead” Vinson.
Well, Eddie “Cleanhead” Vinson affected me because he was a good blues player. That’s the way I play, you know. I used to see him all the time in Cootie Williams’ band. He was
great in Cootie Williams’ band. Then he started doing solo, and I got to see him. He sang a little bit, too, which I’m doing now.
You’ve been doing that for 20 years or so.
Yes. Eddie was a good songwriter, too. He wrote a couple of songs that Miles stole and put his name on.
“Four.” Ha-ha. You know about it, yeah.
“Tune-Up,” yup. Yeah, you know about it. That’s what was happening back then. It’s a different world.
So you did see Cootie Williams coming through...
This was once you got back from the Army.
But when you were there, were you checking Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter

Right. I used to play all of Johnny Hodges’ solos. Benny Carter came through and wrote an arrangement for our college band. We played that. There were some nice cats. Tab Smith came through. At that time, Tab was playing with Count Basie’s band. But he was from Wilson, North Carolina, so he was a North Carolinian.
